questions.q: Why does least squares **square** each residual instead of simply adding the residuals up?
options: Without squaring, positive and negative gaps cancel, so a terrible line could score zero; squaring also punishes big misses more
Squaring makes the arithmetic faster for the computer
Squaring turns the residuals into percentages so they can be compared
Squaring removes the effect of outliers
questions.why: Raw residuals cancel: a line 10 above one point and 10 below another would total zero. Squaring makes every gap count and weights a 4-unit miss four times a 2-unit miss. The tempting idea that squaring tames outliers is backwards: squaring gives far-away points **more** pull, not less.

questions.q: The Hosur plant's cost line is **cost = 17.1 + 5.3 × output** (cost in ₹ lakh, output in thousand units). What does the 17.1 mean?
options: The cost of each extra thousand units
About ₹17 lakh a month of fixed cost incurred even at zero output
The share of cost variation the line explains
A meaningless number that only positions the line
questions.why: The intercept is the predicted cost when output is zero, which here is a real quantity: rent, salaries and standing charges. The 5.3 is the slope (variable cost). It is tempting to dismiss every intercept as meaningless, as in the flat-price example, but whether it means something depends on whether x = 0 is a sensible situation.

questions.q: Using the Hosur line **cost = 17.1 + 5.3 × output**, what is the forecast monthly cost for 4,500 units?
options: ₹23.85 lakh
₹255.6 lakh
₹43.00 lakh
₹40.95 lakh
questions.why: Output is measured in thousands, so x = 4.5: 17.1 + 5.3 × 4.5 = 17.1 + 23.85 = ₹40.95 lakh. ₹23.85 lakh forgets the fixed cost, ₹255.6 lakh plugs in 45 instead of 4.5 (a units slip), and ₹43 lakh is just the observed cost at 5,000 units.

questions.q: The best line through the five Chennai flats is **price = 9 + 4.3 × area** (area in hundreds of sq ft). The couple's 1,100 sq ft flat is listed at ₹62 lakh. What is its residual, and what does it say?
options: −5.7: the line over-predicts, so the flat is cheap
+5.7: the line is wrong and should be refitted through this flat
+5.7: the asking price is about ₹5.7 lakh above what the line predicts
+0.57: the flat is almost exactly fairly priced
questions.why: Predicted price = 9 + 4.3 × 11 = ₹56.3 lakh, and residual = actual − predicted = 62 − 56.3 = +5.7. A positive residual means the line under-predicts, so the listing sits above the market line. Getting the sign backwards (predicted − actual) is the classic slip.

questions.q: You fit a straight line of fuel use on speed and the residual plot goes positive, then negative, then positive again (a U-shape). What should you conclude?
options: The errors are not normal, so only the p-values are affected
The relationship curves, so a straight line is the wrong model; try polynomial terms or trees
There is one outlier that should be deleted
The model is fine because the residuals still add up to zero
questions.why: A systematic pattern in the residuals means the model is missing structure; a U-shape breaks the **L (linear)** assumption. Residuals of a least-squares line always sum to zero, so that fact tells you nothing about whether the shape is right.

questions.q: A sixth sale is added to the five flats: 900 sq ft at ₹90 lakh (probably a typo for ₹40 lakh). Refitting gives slope ≈ 3.44 and intercept ≈ 24.5. Why did one point out of six move the slope so much?
options: Because least squares gives every point exactly equal influence
Because the new point is outside the range of area, so it is an extrapolation
Because the errors are squared, so a far-away point's huge residual dominates the total and drags the line towards it
Because R² dropped, which automatically changes the slope
questions.why: A residual of tens of lakh becomes hundreds once squared, so the fit tilts to shrink it, cutting the slope from 4.3 to about 3.44. The point is not an extrapolation: area 9 sits inside the 6–14 range. R² is a summary of the fit, not something that drives the coefficients.

questions.q: For the five flats, SSE = 6.40 and the total squared deviation from the mean price is 746. The chapter reports R² ≈ 0.991. Which statement about this number is correct?
options: It is measured on the training flats, so it flatters the model; test-set RMSE and R² are the honest check
It proves the model will predict new flats to within 1%
It means area causes 99% of the price
It means 99% of the flats lie exactly on the line
questions.why: R² = 1 − 6.40 / 746 ≈ 0.991 is the share of variation removed **on the data used to fit the line**, which always looks better than on unseen data. It says nothing about causation, and points can all miss the line slightly while R² stays high.

questions.q: Interview question: "Which of the LINE assumptions can you relax if you only care about point predictions, not confidence intervals?"
options: Linearity: the line works for any shape of data
Independence: correlated errors never matter
Equal spread: it is the only assumption that affects the slope
Normality of errors: it mainly matters for confidence intervals and p-values, much less for prediction
questions.why: Normal residuals are needed for the textbook intervals and tests, but least squares still gives sensible predictions without them. Linearity cannot be relaxed: a curved relationship gives systematically wrong predictions. Independence and equal spread mainly affect how much you can trust the uncertainty estimates, not whether a line is the right shape.
